title: How many Fed rate cuts in 2026?
description:
This market will resolve according to the exact amount of cuts of 25 basis points in 2026 by the Fed (including any cuts made during the December meeting).

Emergency rate cuts outside of scheduled FOMC meetings will also count toward the total number of cuts in 2026. This market will remain open until December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM ET, to account for any such emergency actions.

For example, if the Fed cuts rates by 50 bps after a meeting, it would be considered 2 cuts (of 25 bps each).

This market will resolve early to "No" if the specified number of cuts becomes impossible — i.e., if more cuts have already occurred than the strike in question.

Note that cuts between 1–24 bps (inclusive) will also be considered 1 rate cut.

The resolution source for this market will be FOMC statements after meetings scheduled in 2026 according to the official calendar: https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/fomccalendars.htm. The level and change of the target federal funds rate is also published at the official website of the Federal Reserve at https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm.

eventMetadata.context_description:
**Elevated and sticky inflation remains the dominant driver keeping the market-implied probability of zero Fed rate cuts in 2026 at 87.8%.** July 2026 PCE inflation held at 3.7% year-over-year—above the 2% target and slightly hotter than consensus—while core PCE stayed at 3.3%. This followed earlier upward revisions in the June 2026 FOMC Summary of Economic Projections, which lifted the median end-2026 federal funds rate projection to 3.8% from 3.4% in March, signaling policymakers see inflation persisting longer than previously expected amid supply-side pressures and geopolitical energy price effects.

The current target range of 3.50–3.75% has been unchanged since late 2025, and recent labor-market data (July unemployment at 4.1%) show only gradual cooling without signaling recessionary weakness that would justify easing. Trader consensus, reflected in futures pricing, anticipates the Fed will hold steady through year-end or deliver net hikes, consistent with the hawkish tilt in communications and the absence of any near-term cut signals. Key upcoming catalysts include the September FOMC meeting and subsequent inflation and employment releases, which could reinforce or modestly shift these probabilities if data surprise materially lower.
